response:
It takes real self-awareness to recognize your part while also wanting to grow, and that's a strength, not a flaw. When one person yells and the other withdraws, it's a cycle that both people contribute to—so this isn't just "your problem," even if you're working on your piece of it.

A helpful place to start is using "I" statements: instead of "You always yell," try "I feel scared and shut down when the volume rises, and I want us to hear each other." Choosing calmer moments to talk, rather than mid-conflict, can also make it easier to be heard. Writing down your thoughts first sometimes helps if speaking up feels overwhelming.

Because these patterns are deeply rooted, a couples counselor can be genuinely useful in giving you both tools and a safe space to practice. And if his yelling ever feels intimidating or unsafe, please take that seriously and reach out to someone you trust. You deserve to feel heard.
